versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him. 2 When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is the camp of God.” So he named that place Mahanaim.

3 Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom. 4 He instructed them, “You are to say to my master Esau, ‘Your servant Jacob says: I have been staying with Laban and have remained there until now. 5 I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants, and maidservants. I have sent this message to inform my master, so that I may find favor in your sight.’”
6 When the messengers returned to Jacob, they said, “We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you—he and four hundred men with him.”
7 In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps, as well as the flocks and herds and camels. 8 He thought, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.”

9 Then Jacob declared, “O God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, the LORD who told me, ‘Go back to your country and to your kindred, and I will make you prosper,’ 10 I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. Indeed, with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps. 11 Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me. 12 But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.’”

13 Jacob spent the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selected a gift for his brother Esau: 14 200 female goats, 20 male goats, 200 ewes, 20 rams, 15 30 milk camels with their young, 40 cows, 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys, and 10 male donkeys. 16 He entrusted them to his servants in separate herds and told them, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.”

17 He instructed the one in the lead, “When my brother Esau meets you and asks, ‘To whom do you belong, where are you going, and whose animals are these before you?’ 18 then you are to say, ‘They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau. And behold, Jacob is behind us.’”

19 He also instructed the second, the third, and all those following behind the herds: “When you meet Esau, you are to say the same thing to him. 20 You are also to say, ‘Look, your servant Jacob is right behind us.’” For he thought, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.”
21 So Jacob’s gifts went on before him, while he spent the night in the camp.

context_lines: As Jacob continues toward Canaan, God's angels meet him, and he names the place Mahanaim after recognizing God's camp. The encounter recalls the angels in his dream at Bethel when he was leaving the land. Now the assurance of God's presence accompanies his return.

Jacob sends messengers to Esau, using respectful language and asking for favor. They return with news that Esau is approaching with four hundred men. The report does not state Esau's intention, but Jacob remembers the earlier threat and is deeply afraid. He divides his people and animals so that one camp might escape if the other is attacked.

His prayer joins God's promise with an honest admission of fear. He recalls the command to return, acknowledges that he has not earned the kindness shown him, and asks for protection for himself, the mothers, and the children. The man who crossed the Jordan with a staff now has a large household whose future concerns him.

Jacob then sends substantial gifts of livestock ahead in separate groups, instructing the servants to identify them as presents for Esau. He hopes to soften his brother's anger before meeting him. Prayer and practical preparations stand together in the account as the encounter draws near.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read Jacob's prayer as humble dependence on God's promise in a frightening situation. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 32:7, 9–13](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) also regard his efforts toward peace as compatible with trust, rather than assuming that taking practical steps necessarily cancels his prayer.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: Jacob appeals to the kindness God has already shown and the word He has already given. The promise has brought him this far, and he now brings his fear into that relationship. His prayer does not claim that his own worth entitles him to a safe outcome.

The New Testament's invitation in [Hebrews 4:14–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/4.htm) similarly joins acknowledged weakness with confidence in God's mercy. Through Jesus, believers can approach for grace and help in need. The shared theme is dependence on God's faithful care, with room to speak honestly about the danger rather than pretending not to be afraid.
